In juveniles and moulting adults, the rump is pale gray, becoming grey in both phases late in the year.

Juvenile birds are paler and browner than adults.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile has paler underparts, and appears generally duller, especially on the flanks. Juvenile fulvous whistling ducks are very like young lesser whistling ducks, but the crown colour is still a distinction.

chick.notes: The eggs hatch in about 24–29 days, The downy ducklings are grey, with paler upperparts, and a white band on the neck, and weigh 22–38 g (0.78–1.34 oz) within a day of hatching. Like all ducklings, they are precocial and leave the nest after a day or so, but the parents protect them until they fledge around nine weeks later.

juvenile.notes: Adults have variably colored eyes, ranging from yellow to pale brown to yellow brown, while those of juveniles are dark brown. Dark morph juvenile tawny eagles are generally light rufous to rufous brown with creamier lower back to upper tail coverts.

chick.notes: In India, tawny eagles pairs seem to adapt to suboptimal overly sandy habitats by more dispersing nests, and can show similar productivity of chicks per nest as a result. In Hwange National Park, 72.4% of pairs present were thought to breed on average in the course of a year, with an average of 0.61 fledglings produced per effort.
The eggs hatch after approximately 13 days. The chicks are fed by both parents and are brooded by the female for the first five or six days.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are similar to non-breeding adults but have greenish-black legs and duller yellow feet, and may have a certain proportion of greyish or brownish feathers.

chick.notes: The three to five eggs are incubated by both adults for 21 to 25 days before hatching. The young birds are covered in white down feathers, are cared for by both parents and fledge after 40 to 45 days.
Nestlings are fed by both parents and also by helpers, which usually are juveniles from previous clutches. After a little over a month, the nestlings will begin foraging for themselves.

Chicks are precocial, can run as soon as they hatch, and fledge in 56–100 days. Once they are fully grown and independent, chicks of different sexes will separate from their parents to start their own family.

juvenile.notes: The sexes are similar, but the juvenile is spotted with buff above, and is whitish spotted with brown below.
Juvenile and immature plumages differ markedly from the plumage of adults. Immatures have a strongly contrasting golden crown and a rufous or ginger nape and mantle.

chick.notes: Hatching happens at about to 2–3 days apart, with about 24 hours from the first chipping of the egg's surface to complete hatching. Aggression may continue for up to 70 days after hatching.
The juveniles from the first brood have been recorded bringing food to the nestlings of the 2nd brood in Schalow's wheatear.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile lizard buzzard resembles the adult; the only variations are slight brown tinge to the wings with an orange yellow cere and legs.

chick.notes: The clutch size is 1–3 white eggs which are incubated by the female and take 32–34 days before hatching. During this time the male feeds the female and both feed the chicks for the next 40 days.

juvenile.notes: The immature has duller green spots and buff fringes to the feathers.
The plumage of the juvenile is brown, and the eyes are paler than the adult's.

chick.notes: Incubation lasts for 42 to 45 days before the chicks hatch. Siblicide does not normally occur in this taxon, and the parents often successfully rear two or three chicks.
They hatch after 22 to 23 days. The young fledge when aged around 30 days.

juvenile.notes: Immature birds have yellow rather than orange bare skin on their faces, more brownish plumage, shorter tail feathers, and greyish rather than brown irises.

chick.notes: The eggs hatch after around 45 days at intervals of 2–3 days. The adults regurgitate food onto the floor of the nest and then pick up items and pass them to the chicks.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile is mottled brown, buff and white above, with buff edgings to the wing and tail feathers.

chick.notes: Both sexes incubate for about 19 days to hatching. The chicks fledge in another 22 days but are dependent for about eight weeks.

juvenile.notes: Females and immatures are much less striking, with dark brown scaly upperparts, and paler brown scaly underparts.
Juveniles have ochre-buff spots above and scaly brown spots below.
Immature males and females are very similar in appearance to the adult female. However, immature males, much like adult non-breeding males, are slightly larger than adult females.

Although plumage differs between juveniles, males, and females, cinnamon-breasted buntings can be identified by their striped head and cinnamon brown underparts. Juveniles are similar to females but with buffier head stripes and a paler, browner throat.

The juvenile osprey may be identified by buff fringes to the plumage of the upperparts, a buff tone to the underparts, and streaked feathers on the head. During spring, barring on the underwings and flight feathers is a better indicator of a young bird, due to wear on the upperparts.

chick.notes: The eggs are incubated for about 35–43 days to hatching. The newly hatched chicks weigh only 50–60 g (1.8–2.1 oz), but fledge in 8–10 weeks.

juvenile.notes: Steppe eagle juveniles are almost invariably paler than adults, with some ranging overall from umber-brown to tawny-buff but then some are darker and more deeply brown. Juveniles tend to be brown to grey-brown on the upperparts but for generally rufous-buff nape patch (more so on the eastern population).

chick.notes: In several parts of Africa, steppe eagles may routinely visit and feed off of the colonies of the super-abundant bird, the red-billed quelea (Quelea quelea), with a noted focus on picking off the seemingly innumerous nestlings and fledglings of this small passerine. The steppe eagles seldom actively hunted, instead alternating between capturing nestlings from the heronries, especially nearly fledgling-age young of late nesting painted storks (Mycteria leucocephala), and engaging in kleptoparasitism towards other birds of prey, often doing so in groups of about three to nine eagles.
The female lays two to three large white eggs and later the chicks feed by plunging their heads deep into the adult's pouch and taking the partially digested regurgitated fish.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile plumage is similar to the female, but has a finer mottling pattern.

It has long legs that are variable in colour, being dark greenish in juveniles, pink to orange in adults with some males having reddish orange legs only during the breeding season. The plumage of the juveniles resembles the non-breeding adult, but has upperparts with a neat, scale-like pattern with dark feather centres, and a strong buff tinge to the underparts.

chick.notes: Incubation is by the female alone, and the time to hatching is 20–23 days, with a further 25–28 days to fledging. The precocial chicks have buff and chestnut down, streaked and barred with black, and frosted with white; they feed themselves on a variety of small invertebrates, but are brooded by the female.

juvenile.notes: The adult male has a bright red band across its throat (thus the name "cut throat"), while the male juveniles have a slightly duller red band.

chick.notes: A clutch usually consists of 3 to 6 white eggs, which hatch after an incubation period of 12–13 days. The chicks leave the nest after 21–27 days but continue to be fed by their parents for a further three weeks.

juvenile.notes: As seen in about half of the "booted eagle" group, the juvenile crowned eagle has strikingly different looking plumage compared to the adults. A great majority of juveniles have a white head and underside, which contrast with the thighs and legs, which are heavily spotted with black.

chick.notes: While the incubation and nestling stages are about average for a tropical eagle (for example the black-breasted snake-eagle (Circaetus pectoralis), about half the weight of this species, has an incubation/nestling cycle of a similar length), it is the extraordinary post-fledging period of 9–11 months that makes the crowned eagles' breeding cycle so long. When they initially hatch, the young tend to be quite quiet.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are similar to adults but the upper parts have a greenish tinge and more diffuse barring, and both sexes have some red colouring on the crown and nape.

chick.notes: The young owls can fly at around seven weeks of age, but continue to stay with the parents for several weeks after they have fledged.

Chestnut-bellied sandgrouse are sexually mature after one year following hatching. In captivity, incubation is done mainly by the female, with all the young hatching simultaneously after the end of the incubation period.

juvenile.notes: The underparts are also chestnut in the adults, only in juveniles they are white with a chestnut belly patch.

chick.notes: The jacana has evolved a highly unusual polyandrous mating system, meaning that one female mates with multiple males and the male alone cares for the chicks. This means that the rate-limiting factor of the jacana's breeding is the rate at which the males can raise and care for the chicks.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile is similar to the female but the feathers of the brown upperparts have pale centres near the tips giving the bird a speckled appearance.

chick.notes: Females also do all of the feeding, primarily via regurgitation, during the nestling period for the offspring, which is between 14 and 17 days.

juvenile.notes: The female and juvenile plumages are similar to the non-breeding male, but the flight feathers and tail are brown.

chick.notes: Chicks are fed by both sexes, the male often passing food to the female and she then feeds the nestlings. The fledging period is 16 days with the adults accompanying the fledglings, calling loudly if approached.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles look like adults, only darker and plainer, and body feathers have a purplish sheen.
The juvenile resembles the male, but is less glossy than the adults, and has brown rather than dark red eyes.

chick.notes: The female incubates the eggs for 13–14 days, with another 22–28 days to fledge.
Eggs take 26-32 days to hatch.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are more heavily barred above and have buff edges to the wing feathers.
Young birds are very similar to the adults, except for the fact that they are duller and the base of their mandible has brown markings.

chick.notes: The female incubates the eggs for 23 days, and the chicks fledge from the nest about 38–42 days after hatching.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are yellower below than adults.

The juvenile plumage resembles that of the female, but differs by the belly and under wing coverts which are not spotted, but uniformly red brown in colour.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are greyish-brown with a dull, partially bare orange face and a dull yellowish bill.

Alongside parental feeding by regurgitation of fish, parents have also been observed to regurgitate water into the open bills of their nestlings, especially on hot days.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile resembles the adult but is paler.
Sexes are similar, and juveniles are slightly duller than adults.

Females and juveniles have hints of chestnut on their supercilium, shoulders, and throat, by which they may be distinguished from other sparrows, such as the Kenya sparrow and the other rufous sparrows, which are common in much of the chestnut sparrow's range; or the house sparrow, which also occurs in parts of its range.

chick.notes: A chick African hawk-eagle may take just under 2 days to hatch. Newly hatched eaglets are covered in dark grey down with whitish down on abdomen and thighs, with dull yellow cere and feet.

The sexes are similar, but the juvenile is duller and has blackish brown underparts.

chick.notes: The chicks are partly covered with down at hatching, but are not capable of fending for themselves; they become capable of regulating their temperature at 9–12 days and are fully feathered in 13–21 days. juvenile.notes: The sexes are similar, but non-breeding adults and juveniles are browner, with a white belly.

chick.notes: Both male and female birds feed the chicks, providing flies, beetle larvae, lizards, and seeds. The nestling period typically spans from 16 to 22 days.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles have a brown back, duller than adult females, with a rufous wash on the breast.

chick.notes: Despite being bird-eaters and bigger than sociable weavers, the pygmy falcons largely leave the latter alone, though they do occasionally catch and eat nestlings and even adults. Faecal matter is also thought to boost the immune system of chicks as well as signal to conspecifics.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile is similar in appearance to the female, but is browner with more spotting on the mantle, with shorter crest and neck plumes. Male juveniles are larger than females and can be the same overall size as the adult male but tends to be less bulky with a thinner neck, shorter head crest, paler eyes and a darker mantle.

chick.notes: When the chicks hatch, the mother brings them a steady stream of food, most of it soft so the chicks can eat it easily. Captive hatchlings weigh 78 to 116 g (2.8 to 4.1 oz) on their first day but grow quickly.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles have the mantle grey rather than black, and remain in this plumage for a year.
Juveniles have dingy grey wing coverts, with back and scapular feathers vermiculated with reddish-brown. By their first summer, the primaries of juveniles appear very worn and brownish.

chick.notes: Islets improve hatching success by reducing predation. Hatching success varies by site and year, ranging from 54–78% in the Olonne Marsh and 8–59% in the Séné Marshes.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile resembles the adult in plumage, but the areas corresponding to the adult black feathers are browner and less glossy. It could possibly be confused with the juvenile yellow-billed stork, but the latter has paler wings and mantle, a longer bill and white under the wings.

chick.notes: Hatching is asynchronous, and takes place at the end of May. Fledging takes 60 to 71 days, after which the young joins the adults at their feeding grounds.

juvenile.notes: Young birds are dull buff below and on the face and neck, with dull brown upperparts, top of the head and eyestripe. Immature knob-billed ducks look like a large greyish female of the cotton pygmy goose (Nettapus coromandelicus) and may be difficult to tell apart if no other birds are around to compare size and hue.

chick.notes: Chicks join creches soon after hatching, sometimes numbering over 100,000 individuals.

juvenile.notes: Juvenile buzzards are quite similar to adult in the nominate subspecies, being best told apart by having a paler eye, a narrower subterminal band on the tail and underside markings that appear as streaks rather than bars. Furthermore, juveniles may show variable creamy to rufous fringes to upperwing coverts but these also may not be present.

chick.notes: Here, the mean number of fledglings were 1.75 against 0.82–1.41 in other parts of Britain. It was found in the English Midlands that breeding success both by measure of clutch size and mean number of fledglings, was relatively high due to high prey populations.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile is very distinct from the adults of the species. Juveniles of the bateleur have a longer tail than mature birds.

chick.notes: It is estimated that the bateleur produces a mean of 0.47 chicks per nest per year.

juvenile.notes: The sexes are similar, but juveniles are duller than adults and have a brown bill.

The juvenile is similar in appearance and colour but tends to have very sparse white feather bases, with birds from south of the range apparently showing heavier white speckling, especially on the abdomen and head. This species has a large head and bare legs, which serve to distinguish it from other brownish medium-sized eagles in Africa, although a juvenile bateleur could be confused with one in poor light, but its colour is more varying, its eyes brown and the species has a shorter tail and shorter legs.

chick.notes: The eggs are incubated by both parents for up to 29 days, and upon hatching the young birds are cared for by both parents for around 20 to 30 days.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile is similar to adults, with the plumage being more brown, especially on wing-coverts.

Juveniles are similar to the adult female, but deeper brown below and paler above, with paler and less defined supercilia. Juveniles have broader buff feather edges, and tend to have looser, scruffier plumage, like moulting adults.

chick.notes: House sparrows can breed in the breeding season immediately following their hatching, and sometimes attempt to do so. Birds breeding for the first time are rarely successful in raising young, and reproductive success increases with age, as older birds breed earlier in the breeding season, and fledge more young.

juvenile.notes: Young birds miss the black markings entirely, which instead are the same brownish shade as the mantle and wings. The bill of juveniles is horn-colored and the iris is dark brown.

chick.notes: Nests have two downward-facing entrances, one of which is closed as soon as the eggs are laid until the moment the youngsters fledge.

juvenile.notes: Adult African green pigeons have maroon patches on the top of their wings and the juveniles have an olive color.

Juveniles have black-bordered tawny spots on upperparts, mottled buff and black on throats and breasts.

chick.notes: The chicks are buff coloured and have black stripes running along their length.

juvenile.notes: As adults, their beaks are black but as juveniles, their beaks are grey. Females and juveniles are more brown on the front of their body.
Like many shrike species the appearance of the adults is similar between the sexes but strikingly different in juvenile birds.
The juvenile can be told by its white rump.
The back is spotted white to varying extents, being maximal in the breeding adult, and less in winter and young birds.

chick.notes: The clutch takes about three weeks to hatch.

juvenile.notes: Juvenile birds have a blotched breast, scalloping on the upperparts and some streaking on the flanks.
Juveniles and immature birds do not have a mask on the dark-yellowish green head.

Males in immature and winter plumage are similar to females, except that adult males retain the white wing patches all year round. Though fairly similar to females and immatures of the European stonechat (S. rubicola), the whinchat can readily be distinguished by its conspicuous supercilium and whiter belly, and also in western Europe, by being paler overall than the western European stonechat subspecies S. rubicola hibernans.

chick.notes: There is only one narrow aperture, just big enough for the male to transfer food to the mother and chicks. When the chicks and the female are too big for the nest, the mother breaks out and rebuilds the wall.

juvenile.notes: Sexes are similar, but young birds have a brown cap and a pale yellow bill.

chick.notes: Incubation occurs for 12–15 days by the female but both parents feed the nestlings. The fledgling period spans 13–17 days but the nestlings can remain dependent on the female for some time after this period.

Once the chick hatches, both parents will feed and tend to it for about 150 days when it fledges. Young remain dependent on their parents after fledging, not reaching independence until the next breeding season.

juvenile.notes: The Juvenile is brown with a white belly; eyes brown, becoming orange-red in as the bird matures. Exceptional young birds are entirely white below, including chin and throat.
Juveniles are like females, but mostly unbarred tawny-brown with a reddish-brown bill.

chick.notes: Incubation is about 30 days by the mother and the fledgling period is 86 days and only the mother takes care of the young.

juvenile.notes: The juveniles are similar to the adults, but the plumage is lighter in colour and the crest is not developed and their eyes are grey.
Immature birds are like the female but plainer and without a supercilium.
The juvenile resembles the female.

chick.notes: The chicks are fed by both parents until fledging time, and the chicks will for a time return to the nest to roost.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles have a browner breast than adults and buff tips to feathers. Juvenile primary feathers are retained after the post-juvenile moult.

chick.notes: Chicks are fiercely defended by the parents from avian predators including African fish-eagles, harriers, and coucals. Chicks are precocial, leaving the nest only a few hours after hatching, and fledge approximately two months after hatching.

juvenile.notes: The pre-juvenile moult of the chick occurs at the nest site from late June to July. The juvenile looks similar to the adult non-breeding plumage, but the wear marks and fringing on its feathers are more evenly spread out, resulting in a scaly and more buff-tinged appearance, and the tail feathers are slimmer.

chick.notes: At birth, the nestlings are relatively mature and mobile, covered with down, and begin to wander from the nest after drying. On average, the nestling weighs 8.2 g, with a bill length of 10.8 mm, a tarsus length of 23.2 mm, and a wingspan of 17 mm.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are duller and browner.

Both subspecies have long, black outermost tail streamers that are absent in juveniles. Juveniles, immatures and adults have the largest alula feather dark blue, but the primary coverts and rest of the alula azure.
The sexes are similar, but juveniles have a brown crown, white head sides, and grey breast.

The rufous is replaced by a dirty brownish grey in non-breeding and juvenile birds. Juvenile birds have a yellow bill with a small black tip, and black and white streaks on the cheeks and sides of the neck as seen below.
Juveniles have tails like the adults, but lack a supercilium. Immatures are like adults but retain some buff-tipped greater wing coverts.

chick.notes: Both parents will feed the nestlings during the subsequent 14 to 18 days, and for 5 to 7 weeks after they leave nest.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles look similar to adults, but are paler.

chick.notes: Although they can sometimes replace clutches, often only around 25% of eggs succeed in hatching due to various environmental conditions or predation. Around 62% of fledglings who successfully leave the nest survive to adulthood.

juvenile.notes: Juvenile resembles a non-breeding adult, but with less variation in the feather colours.

By three weeks, the young bird acquires black scapulars and flight feathers. By the time it fledges, the juvenile bird's plumage is similar to that of the adult, though its black feathers are often tinged with brown, and its beak and legs are a duller brownish-red or orange.

chick.notes: Larger nests are associated with greater numbers of young successfully fledged, and appear to be sought after. Incubation begins as soon as the first egg is laid, so the brood hatches asynchronously, beginning 33 to 34 days later.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile, which takes 3–4 years to mature, is brown with yellow eye-patches. Juveniles on the other hand are predominately brown with partially black wings and take a lengthy three to four years to make the transition into the adult plumage.

chick.notes: Normally around 85 to 90 days after hatching, the young brown chicks will fledge.

juvenile.notes: The white plumage of immature birds is often mixed with black.

chick.notes: Incubation is 18–19 days and the young are usually fledged by around 45 days.

juvenile.notes: In immature birds, the belly is more buff than yellow and the dark breast band less distinct. Its more orange throat helps distinguish it from the yellow-throated longclaw and Abyssinian longclaw, however the throats of female and older immature Pangani longclaws can be more yellow.

chick.notes: In India, nestlings have been found to be prone to maggot infestations (probably by Protocalliphora species) and in some areas to leeches.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are a paler rufous colour.

chick.notes: Incubation starts with the first egg so that the young hatch asynchronously and if there is a food shortage then siblicide occurs. Five weeks after the eggs hatch, the young will leave the nest and are able to fly two weeks later.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles of the species are duller; their feathers are dark grey.

chick.notes: At first, adult birds feed the hatchlings insects, then later mostly fruit. The hatchlings' parents and the helpers remove faeces from the nest.

juvenile.notes: Immature black-winged stilt are grey and have a markedly sandy hue on their wings, with light feather fringes appearing as a whitish line in flight.

Immature birds independent from their parents have lost most of the mottling (except on the wing coverts) and barring, but their wing stripe and underside are still dull white, shading to brown on the flanks; any white tail feather tips appear at this stage.

chick.notes: The eggs hatch after 14–16 days, and nestlings take again as long to fledge.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile is mainly brown–black above, with barring on the head and buff tips to the shoulder feathers.

The juvenile has darker, brownish underparts that are palest at the rump, center of the belly, and uppertail coverts. Its underparts and back are initially browner and darker than those of the Dalmatian pelican, and the underwing is strongly patterned, similar to the juvenile brown pelican.

chick.notes: The chicks are naked when they hatch but quickly sprout blackish-brown down. The colony gathers in "pods" around 20 to 25 days after the eggs hatch.

juvenile.notes: All are tawny brown above and on the breast and white on the belly, with cream-coloured legs; juveniles have light brown necks and heads, and adults have blue-grey necks.

chick.notes: Nests are usually a simple unlined scrape in the ground and situated in or under vegetation so that the eggs, chicks, and female can be hidden from predators. In certain countries, white-bellied bustard chicks have been successfully raised until adulthood in captivity (mostly during the 1990's).

juvenile.notes: Juvenile grey kestrels are browner than the adults with a greenish cere and greenish around the eye. Juvenile Dickinson's kestrels are similar but have a barred tail and a more strongly barred underwing.
Juveniles are similar to females, but usually have less yellow, particularly on the shoulders. Juveniles of this morph may look entirely black in flight.

chick.notes: They often lay 1 to 2 eggs and after the eggs have hatched the new chicks are fed and brooded mainly by the female for a period of 16 to 21 days. The nests that these chicks live in over this period of time are built by the female only and it takes her anywhere between 5 and 15 days before the chicks are born.

juvenile.notes: Sexes are similar, but young birds have pale brown instead of grey, and dark brown replacing black.
Juveniles are dull brown above with a pale stripe over the eye. They are indistinguishable from some juvenile dark chanting goshawks except for the less barred undertail coverts and rump.
Juveniles are brown with little gloss, and have short tails.

chick.notes: Only one parent, probably the female, incubates for 14–19 days to hatching, with a further 24–27 days until the young fledge.

juvenile.notes: The cere and the legs are yellow in immatures and the plumage is generally browner, with the pale birds having untidier barring on the chest than the adult.
The juvenile is similar to the adult female.
The juveniles are quite different, with charcoal grey upperparts and chestnut brown lowerparts.
Juveniles lack the red cap and shoulders of the adults, have dark spotting on the breast, and white spots on the dark brown upperparts.
An immature is duller and lacks the semi-collar of an adult.

chick.notes: Chicks are fed regurgitated food by both parents and fledge after about 16 days.

juvenile.notes: It is very pale and mainly grey, with a browner back and pink on the bill (young birds lack the pink).
The juvenile is brownish with brown wings and tail and is heavily barred with grey.

chick.notes: Incubation begins as soon as the first egg is laid, so the chicks are born asynchronously. The chicks hatch with a covering of downy feathers.

juvenile.notes: Young birds are like the female, but browner on the back.

The sexes are similar in appearance, and the juveniles can be distinguished from adults by their lack of elongated central tail feathers and the pinkish brown coloration of their mantle, chest to belly, and flanks.
The male is mainly glossy black with white streaking; females and immature birds are browner.
The juveniles and females are notoriously difficult to identify in the field, appearing identical to the juveniles and females of several other bishops and widowbirds as well as some seedeaters.
The bill is black in young birds and reddish-orange in adults; the legs are bright red. Sexes are similar, but juveniles are a duller version of the adult.

Juvenile gull-billed terns have a fainter mask, but otherwise look much like winter adults. Juvenile Sandwich terns have a short bill, and are frequently mistaken for gull-billed tern where the latter species is uncommon, such as North Sea coasts.
Sexes are similar, but the juvenile is a drabber version of the adult, with a pale breast.

The juvenile is browner and has a paler rufous face and whiter underparts. In Africa the short tail streamers of the juvenile barn swallow invite confusion with juvenile red-chested swallow (Hirundo lucida), but the latter has a narrower breast band and more white in the tail.

chick.notes: The incubation period is normally 14–19 days, with another 18–23 days before the altricial chicks fledge. The fledged young stay with, and are fed by, the parents for about a week after leaving the nest.

A captive female buff-crested bustards has been observed carrying her newborn chicks in attempts to deliberately displace them. The hen carried one chick at a time under her wing to relocate it, then dropped it at a desired location.

juvenile.notes: Older nestlings have a horn-coloured bill with a hint of lavender, though it turns orange-purple before the post-juvenile moult. Young birds change feathers two to three months after hatching, after which the plumage resembles that of non-breeding adults, although the head is grey, the cheeks whitish, and wing coverts and flight feathers have buff margins.

chick.notes: After the chicks hatch, they are fed for some days with protein-rich insects. Later the nestlings mainly get seeds.

juvenile.notes: Young birds lack the chequered neck markings.
Juveniles are duller with little or no red on the belly, fainter dark barring and a black bill.
Juvenile birds are greyer, while birds of the nominate subspecies show grey flanks.
In the female and young birds the upperparts are brown and vermiculated.
The sexes are alike, but the young bird is browner and has a smaller bill.

chick.notes: The female lays two to three eggs in a small nest made of sticks; eggs hatch after an incubation period of 30 days.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile is paler than the adult, has a whitish breast, and lacks the facial shield; the adult's black plumage develops when about 3–4 months old, but the white shield is only fully developed at about one year old, some time later.

chick.notes: The eggs are incubated by both sexes for 18–25 days and hatch asynchronously. The downy precocial chicks leave the nest after one day and are then fed and cared for by both parents for 55–60 days.

juvenile.notes: Immature birds resemble females, but have brownish bills and brown irides, while the upperparts and flanks are still greyer, and the underparts and edges of the wing feathers are yet more buffy.

chick.notes: Both parents rear the chicks, which leave the nest after some 18 days.

juvenile.notes: Sexes are similar, but the juvenile is a drabber version of the adult.

chick.notes: They hatch after 17 to 19 days. The nestlings fledge after 26 to 27 days.
These fledge after 40–50 days, become independent usually a few weeks thereafter, and may raise their first brood the next spring.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are similar to adults but the head and back spots may be lacking or much reduced and the false 'face' is very obvious.

chick.notes: During the three year period, no scimitarbills hatched, while 7 out of a total of 12 of the parasitic honeyguide eggs successfully fledged. Later from August 2012-September 2014, four clutches (12 eggs total) were laid without any honeyguides, and all but one individual was successfully fledged.
The eggs are reportedly laid at up to 7 day intervals and may take up nearly seven days as well between hatching. On average at hatching, the young weigh about 60 to 70 g (2.1 to 2.5 oz).

The breeding season of the black kite in India begins in winter (mainly January and February), the young birds fledging before the monsoons. Both the male and female take part in nest building, incubation and care of chicks.

juvenile.notes: Sexes are similar, and young birds differ mainly in their shorter tails.
Immature birds have dull grey-brown plumage on their heads, wings, and backs, with numerous pale "teardrop" spots. The young birds have orange eyes and duller yellowish-green legs.
Juveniles have a red bill, streaky throat and a white wing-bar.

The southern ground hornbill is black with vivid red patches of bare skin on the face and throat (yellow in juvenile birds)—as well as being one of few birds with eyelashes—which are believed to keep dust out of the birds' eyes while they forage during the dry season. Juveniles to six years old lack the prominent red pouch, having a duller patch of grey in its place.

chick.notes: In captivity, a maximum lifespan of 70 years is recorded, and it is generally believed that the life expectancy of a bird that survives long enough to fledge is as high as thirty years or more, which is comparable to that of more famously long-lived birds like the wandering albatross. One to three eggs are laid at the beginning of the wet season, but siblicide ensures that only one nestling is ever fledged.

juvenile.notes: Juveniles are blackish-brown with buff scaling.
The bill is brown in young birds, but becomes black by the time a bird fledges.

chick.notes: Incubation takes around 30 days from the first egg being laid to hatching, eggs are laid with intervals of one to three days, and they hatch asynchronously. The young hatch covered with grey down.

juvenile.notes: The juvenile augur buzzard is mainly brown above and rufous brown below and on the tail. Although not as dark as the adult on the back and upperwing coverts, it is usually noticeably darker than a juvenile steppe buzzard.
The sexes are similar, but immatures are browner than adults and lack the red eye patches.

chick.notes: Both parents feed the chicks which fledge at about three weeks old.

juvenile.notes: The female is brown above with white upper tail coverts, hence females and the similar juveniles are often called "ringtails".
Young birds are duller, greyer and less yellow below than the adults.
In immature birds the adult's black stripe on the head is grey, and the white face paler grey; they are generally duller in appearance than adults, with only a small, dark grey crest.

chick.notes: At first, the chicks seize the adult's bill from the side and extract regurgitated food from it. Later, the adult disgorges the food at the nest and the chicks squabble for possession.

juvenile.notes: The sexes are similar, but the juvenile has duller yellow underparts than the adult.
The sexes are alike, but the juvenile has browner plumage, a brown iris and a dull yellow lower mandible.
Juveniles are paler and browner, darkening as they mature.
The sexes are similar, but juveniles are duller than adults.
Immature birds resemble females but have distinct white tips to the tertials (inner wing), and less distinct gape and eye flanges.

chick.notes: The chicks have creamy buff down, featuring both light and dark markings.

juvenile.notes: Sexes are similar, but juveniles have dirty white plumage, a smaller bill and some feathering on the neck, greenish-brown scapulars and more black on the primary coverts.

chick.notes: After hatching, one parent continuously stays at the nest for the first seven days. Chicks fledge after 35 to 40 days and are independent after 44 to 48 days, reaching sexual maturity one to five years after hatching.
The female incubates the eggs for about 28 days and the chicks leave the nest about 63 days after hatching.

juvenile.notes: Immature birds have olive-brown upperparts with a white rump, yellow throat and upper breast.

chick.notes: The chick has a membranous hook on the bill that it uses, while still blind and featherless, to kill the host's young outright or by repeated wounds.
Usually, three or four eggs are incubated about 18–19 days and hatchlings are fledged by around 38 days. Typically, only three nestlings survive.
